composition: Nominal composition Fe–28Mn–9Al–1.2C–3Cr (wt%), i.e. an austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel with 3 wt% Cr addition. The ingot was made from a high-purity elemental charge: Fe 99.99%, Mn 99.9%, Al 99.9%, C 99.8% and Cr 99.9%. The actual (ICP-measured) composition of this strip is Fe balance, Mn 27.6, Al 8.4, C 1.3 and Cr 2.8 wt% — the measured Cr content is close to the 3 wt% target. Mn and C provide austenite stabilization and solid-solution strengthening, Al lowers density, C is the source of κ-carbide precipitation, and Cr is the variable element added to modify κ-carbide precipitation, ferrite fraction and dislocation density. Its measured average density is 6.45 g/cm3, slightly below the 6.49 g/cm3 of the Cr-free strip.
conclusions: Within the Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C–(0, 3, 6, 9)Cr near-rapidly solidified strip series, the as-cast 3Cr strip illustrates the first stage of the non-linear Cr effect on strength. Cr addition raises the δ-ferrite fraction (10.2 → 11.4 vol% from 0Cr to 3Cr) while suppressing κ-carbide precipitation and increasing the austenite dislocation density; these competing effects make the yield strength first fall (3Cr, 617 MPa, the minimum of the series) and then rise again beyond the Cr-free level (6Cr 652 MPa, 9Cr 740 MPa), while total elongation decreases monotonically with Cr (40.8 → 33.2 → 31.6 → 20.3 %). The strip therefore shows a reduced yield strength (−15 % vs 0Cr) and reduced elongation, but a higher steady-stage strain-hardening rate (2048 MPa) and UTS of 896 MPa. The study concludes that the ductility loss of Cr-containing strips originates from the increased dislocation density and larger δ-ferrite/phase-interface fraction (with Cr23C6 grain-boundary carbides dominating the loss in 9Cr), not from casting defects or from κ-carbide coarsening. Practically, the as-cast 3Cr strip demonstrates that Cr is not a simple strengthening addition under near-rapid solidification: it trades yield strength and ductility for improved strain hardening, and the composition is better exploited through subsequent annealing, which restores elongation in Cr-containing strips while the Cr-free strip loses ductility.
mechanisms: Cr addition expands the solid solubility of Al and C in the Fe–Mn–Al–C steel and lowers the driving force for κ-carbide formation, so the higher the Cr content the less κ-carbide precipitates; in the as-cast 3Cr strip this appears as only a very weak κ-carbide superlattice with carbides too small to resolve by TEM.

Reduced κ-carbide precipitation lowers the yield strength (the 3Cr strip reaches the minimum of the series at 617 MPa, below 724 MPa for 0Cr), because nano-scale κ-carbides are a main precipitation-strengthening contributor in these steels.

Because κ-carbides obstruct dislocation glide, their reduced precipitation in Cr-containing strips leads to a higher strain-hardening rate (2048 MPa for 3Cr vs 1626 MPa for 0Cr), whereas the glide-plane softening effect of nano κ-carbides depresses the strain-hardening rate of the Cr-free as-cast strip.

Under the same solidification condition the residual thermal stress from rapid cooling is similar for all strips, but the reduction in fraction/size of nano κ-carbides increases the ability to form dislocations under that stress, so as-cast Cr-containing strips (3Cr, 6Cr) develop a higher austenite dislocation density — confirmed both by TEM and by their higher strain-hardening rate.
An increasing δ-ferrite fraction in Cr-containing strips provides more phase-interface area that can block dislocation propagation, which acts to decrease plasticity.

The higher dislocation density inherited from near-rapid solidification in the Cr-containing strips is one of the main factors reducing their ductility, explaining why the 3Cr strip (33.2 %) is less ductile than the Cr-free strip (40.8 %) despite having fewer/less-coarsened κ-carbides.

Casting porosity is not responsible for the ductility loss: the large centrifugal force gives ample melt feeding and the strips are almost free of casting defects, and any residual defects are randomly distributed.

Annealing at 550 °C promotes κ-carbide precipitation (κ(111) peak at 41.4° appears only in the Cr-free annealed strip) and reduces dislocation density; since Cr still suppresses κ-carbides, Cr-containing strips gain much less yield-strength increment but recover elongation (3Cr: +151 MPa YS, +4.2 % total elongation after 550 °C/5 h), the elongation gain being attributed to dislocation reduction.

Deformation of the austenite proceeds by slip bands as well as dislocations: shearing of κ-carbides by dislocations lets subsequent dislocations cut through the sheared carbides easily, so larger κ-carbides localize shearing and give wide slip-band spacing, while finer/fewer κ-carbides allow multi-directional shearing and narrower slip-band spacing that correlates with higher strain-hardening rate.

The initial dislocation density also controls elongation independently of slip-band formation, which is why a fine slip-band structure does not automatically translate into high ductility in this austenitic low-density steel (dynamic slip band refinement is interfered with by pre-existing dislocations).
microstructure: Two-phase γ + δ microstructure. Austenite (γ, fcc) is the continuous major matrix phase with a lattice constant of 3.56 Å (from XRD); δ-ferrite (bcc) forms 11.4 vol% of dispersed second-phase particles that are uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix and located at the centres of austenite grains, consistent with the FA solidification mode L → L+δ → L+δ+γ → δ+γ. Relative to the Cr-free strip, the 3Cr ferrite particles are larger and more abundant and change from rod-like to partly block-like with dendritic outlines, locally aligned in rows (compare 10.2 vol% and rod-like ferrite in 0Cr). The austenite contains a dense tangled dislocation network, denser than in the Cr-free as-cast strip. κ-carbide precipitation in the austenite is strongly suppressed: only a very weak κ-carbide superlattice is present in the austenite SADP, and the carbides are too small to be identified by TEM (no κ-carbide superlattice at all in 9Cr). The ferrite shows no superlattice and almost clean features without evident secondary phases — DO3 appears only in the 6Cr and 9Cr strips, and Cr23C6 grain-boundary carbides form only in the 9Cr strip. No quantitative grain size or texture data are reported for this strip.
processing: Two-step route ending in the as-cast state. (1) Melting: an alloy ingot was prepared from the high-purity elemental charge and reheated to melt by an induction coil. (2) Near-rapid solidification / centrifugal casting: the liquid metal was poured into a copper mold rotating at 600 r/min in an Ar atmosphere, with a calculated maximum cooling rate of about 5×10^3 K/s, yielding strips of (60–80) mm × 60 mm × 2.5 mm. The as-cast strip is the terminal state of this sample — no post-solidification heat treatment was applied. The higher feeding capacity of the melt under the large centrifugal force leaves the strips almost free of casting defects, with any residual defects randomly distributed. In the parent study this as-cast strip is also the precursor of the annealed 550 °C/5 h (and 1 h / 9 h) condition used to probe the annealing response of the 3Cr composition.
properties: Uniaxial tensile properties (room temperature; gauge 20 mm × 4 mm × 1 mm; strain rate 1×10^-3 s^-1 on an MTS Criterion Model 44, 10 kN; averaged over 3 measurements): yield strength 617 ± 4 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 896 ± 28 MPa, total elongation 33.2 ± 7 %, and an average steady-stage strain-hardening rate of 2048 MPa. The engineering curve of the 3Cr strip ends near 40 % strain with UTS below 1000 MPa. Physical: measured average density 6.45 g/cm3 (water-displacement, SJ-600G analyzer). Compared with the Cr-free as-cast strip of the same series, this sample has a lower yield strength (617 ± 4 vs 724 ± 16 MPa, ≈ −15 %) and lower total elongation (33.2 ± 7 % vs 40.8 ± 8 %), but a higher steady-stage strain-hardening rate (2048 vs 1626 MPa). Characterization techniques applied to this strip: XRD (D/Max-2200, Cu target, 40 kV/40 mA, 4°/min, 2θ = 30–100°), optical microscopy (Zeiss Axio imager A2m), TEM with selected-area diffraction in BF/DF mode (JEM-2100F, 200 kV), uniaxial tensile testing, ICP mass spectrometry for composition, and Archimedes/water-displacement density measurement.
summary: As-cast Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C–3Cr (wt%) austenitic low-density steel strip, produced by centrifugal casting into a copper mold under near-rapid solidification (Ar atmosphere, ~5×10^3 K/s) and tested without any post-solidification heat treatment. The strip is a two-phase γ + δ microstructure (austenite matrix with 11.4 vol% dispersed δ-ferrite) and is one member of the Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C–(0, 3, 6, 9)Cr series used to establish how Cr addition changes ferrite fraction, κ-carbide precipitation, dislocation density and the resulting strength–ductility balance.
unmapped: The as-cast 3Cr strip is the precursor of the annealed 550 °C/5 h 3Cr condition; its measured annealed response is YS 768 ± 9 MPa and UTS 915 ± 23 MPa with total elongation 37.4 ± 5 %, i.e. +151 MPa in yield strength and +4.2 % in elongation after annealing. A separate annealing-time series on the 3Cr composition at 550 °C (1 h, 5 h, 9 h) showed elongation increasing with time while yield strength changed little after the first hour, indicating κ-carbides precipitate mainly within the first hour whereas dislocation recovery needs longer times — longer annealing risks coarsening the κ-carbides, so the anneal time must be optimized.

Slip-band statistics (average spacing and width after tensile fracture, and the dynamic slip band refinement argument) were only analysed in the paper for the 0Cr and 6Cr strips, not for the 3Cr strip, so they are cited here only as the general deformation mechanism of the series.
The paper reports no quantitative interface characterization (coherency, boundary type) and no grain-size or texture data specific to the as-cast 3Cr strip.
